Signs in a Matrix

InvariantsArithmeticLogic
Game: Make every row total and every column total zero or more.
How to play: Press a total to turn every number in its row or column from plus to minus and back.
Look for the math

Given any rectangular array of numbers, reverse the signs of whole rows or columns to make every row sum and every column sum non-negative. The puzzle is in Peter Winkler's Mathematical Puzzles. A natural plan is to keep flipping a line whose sum is negative. But fixing a row can spoil some columns, and fixing those can spoil rows again. Why should it ever stop?

Something that only grows

Watch the total of all the numbers (Σ, in the corner). Flipping a line whose sum is −s turns that part of the total from −s into +s, so the total rises by exactly 2s > 0. Each such flip makes the total strictly bigger. This is a monovariant: a quantity that only moves one way.

Why it must stop

Flipping only changes signs, so the grid always shows the original numbers with some signs reversed. For an m × n grid that is at most 2m+n sign choices (and only half as many different grids, since flipping everything changes nothing). So the total can take only finitely many values, and a total that keeps strictly rising must stop. When no flip of a negative line is possible, no sum is negative: done. This is the extremal principle at work.

What was checked

The logic test flipped negative lines until none was left on 5,000 random grids of every size up to 15 × 15, and it always ended with every sum non-negative. On every small grid tried, flipping negative lines in any order always raised the total.

Flip lines with positive sums on purpose. The total goes down. Can you still finish?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
